Highly recommend this one. Smooth controls and easy to get into with a ton of different characters and abilities to choose from. The graphics are top-notch and really bring the world to life, and the map I tried was well-designed with a good balance of open spaces and tight corridors for some intense battles. Tip: collect those gems fast as you find the next player to fight. Matchmaking does a good job of finding players of similar skill levels, so you can expect some competitive and enjoyable matches. I've been having a blast with this game and I think any casual fighter fan will too. Can’t wait to try 3v3 mode too. Do yourself a favor and give Fallen Arena a try!

After playing this game for 34 minutes and winning MVP multiple times, it is nice to say that there is a game that is intense and tactical that runs over a short duration. I love the characters, the animations, the weapon selection and cannot wait for more maps and new utility within E4C: Fallen Arena. It's nice to see that the ping and hit rates are not significantly disadvantaged based on my location (Australia) like some other MMORPGs. Although the movements and lag/reaction time is evident for some players based on location, I believe the concept of the game is excellent and cannot wait to be a long-term E4C player and NFT holder by unlocking new weapons and rewards. Overall I'd rate the game 4/5 as it stands currently.
I really enjoy the game because it has good graphics and is easy to learn. It also has the option to upgrade weapons and customize characters. I would definitely recommend giving it a try.

Also, if you like sliding on ice, this is also a game for you!. So far I have been able to play with tons of AIs, just wondering why I can not add AI's as friends. Oh as an important note. This means you don't know what you are getting, and it's always in small quantities. So far I had played like 3 hours, and unlock battle-pass tier 23 if I'm not mistaken. No more challenges/quest to do, in order to gain more battle-pass points. One amazing feature is that some characters looks like they are on a T-Pose must of the time. XD I would suggest adding more actions to the characters, right now you only have one action for attacking, and only one skill option. Also there should be different kinds of power ups. the one available are not enough. and also adding secondary objectives, not just hitting people. There are a lot of things to improve, and also to add. But one thing I would suggest it's to change the concept of a Lag Simulator and create/add real movement, and make the game more responsive.

Fallen Arena, developed and published by Ambrus Studio, is a compact multiplayer arena brawler that builds its identity around quick matches, accessible mechanics, and a constant push-and-pull between power and vulnerability. Rather than leaning on a deep narrative or world-building, it uses a light sci-fi premise involving a mysterious meteorite and energy crystals as a functional setup for competitive encounters. The real focus is on moment-to-moment action, where players are dropped into enclosed arenas and immediately pushed into conflict with others over limited resources. The defining mechanic revolves around collecting crystals scattered throughout the arena. These crystals act as both a score system and a direct modifier of your character’s strength. As you gather more, your character grows larger and gains a noticeable combat advantage, particularly in reach and damage potential. However, this increase in power comes with a trade-off: reduced mobility. This creates a dynamic where players must constantly decide whether to play aggressively and risk becoming a slower, more obvious target, or remain nimble and opportunistic. It’s a simple idea, but it injects a layer of strategy into what might otherwise be a straightforward brawler, especially in matches where timing and positioning become just as important as raw combat ability. The arenas themselves are designed to keep players moving and reacting rather than settling into predictable patterns. Environmental hazards are frequently introduced, ranging from damaging zones and creeping dangers to sudden disruptive elements that can turn the tide of a match in seconds. These features ensure that no single strategy remains dominant for long, as players are forced to adapt not only to their opponents but also to the shifting conditions of the battlefield. The relatively small size of the maps contributes to the intensity, keeping encounters frequent and ensuring that matches rarely lose momentum. Character selection adds another layer of variation, with different heroes offering distinct abilities and playstyles. Some characters are better suited for direct confrontation, while others thrive on mobility or indirect tactics. This diversity encourages experimentation, allowing players to find approaches that match their preferred style of play. While the differences between characters are meaningful, the overall system remains easy to grasp, which helps maintain the game’s accessible nature. Matches are typically short, making it easy to jump in and out without a significant time commitment, which suits the game’s design philosophy of fast, repeatable sessions. That said, the simplicity that makes Fallen Arena approachable can also limit its long-term appeal. The core gameplay loop, while engaging in short bursts, doesn’t evolve significantly over time. Without a deeper progression system or a wider variety of modes, the experience can begin to feel repetitive after extended play. The reliance on an active player base also means that match quality can fluctuate depending on population and connectivity, which can impact the consistency of the experience. Visually, the game opts for a clean and functional style that prioritizes readability over detail. Characters are clearly defined, and effects are easy to track even during chaotic encounters, which is essential for a competitive setting. While it lacks the visual polish of larger productions, the presentation serves its purpose well. Audio design follows a similar approach, focusing on responsiveness and feedback rather than atmosphere, ensuring players can quickly interpret what’s happening during fast-paced matches. In the end, Fallen Arena delivers a straightforward but enjoyable multiplayer experience built around a clever risk-reward system and consistently active gameplay. It doesn’t attempt to offer deep systems or a richly developed world, but it succeeds in providing a fast, competitive environment that works best in short sessions. For players looking for an easy-to-learn arena brawler with a bit of strategic nuance, it offers a solid, if somewhat limited, experience. Rating: 7/10
